paragraphs: An Experimental Machine Learning Workflow for Telemedicine Request Urgency Assessment, Statistical Hypothesis Testing, and Interactive Streamlit Dashboard Development
Nexora Care is a healthcare technology company developing Nexora Care Flow, an integrated platform designed to improve healthcare operations and patient care coordination.

The company was established after identifying challenges within hospital environments, where healthcare professionals often had to switch between multiple disconnected systems to access patient records, manage appointments, coordinate telemedicine consultations, and monitor healthcare resources.

Nexora Care Flow addresses these challenges by bringing essential healthcare operations into one connected platform. Its core capabilities include patient records management, appointment scheduling, treatment workflows, telemedicine, care coordination, staff management, and healthcare analytics.
The platform primarily serves small-to-medium-sized clinics and healthcare provider networks, supporting clinic administrators, nurses, physicians, and patients.
Nexora Care is currently expanding its platform capabilities and exploring opportunities to leverage data analytics and machine learning to improve healthcare operations and patient experiences.
One of the challenges identified within Nexora Care's telemedicine workflow is the prioritization of incoming patient requests.
The current first-come-first-served approach means that requests may be handled according to submission time rather than the potential urgency of the symptoms reported.
This creates a situation where patients with minor complaints may remain ahead of patients reporting symptoms that require more urgent clinical attention.

For example, a patient reporting a mild headache may submit a request before another patient experiencing chest discomfort or breathing difficulties. Under a strictly chronological queue, the second patient may have to wait longer despite potentially requiring more immediate attention.

Nexora Care therefore seeks to explore how statistical analysis and machine learning can support telemedicine request prioritization by investigating patterns in patient intake information and estimating the urgency of incoming requests.
The company also requires an interactive analytical dashboard through which relevant patient patterns, statistical findings, model performance, and prioritization insights can be explored.
The project focuses on developing a machine learning classification model that estimates the urgency of incoming telemedicine requests based on patient intake information.

The model will use relevant patient characteristics, reported symptoms, symptom severity, symptom duration, medical history, and available vital signs to classify requests into four urgency categories:
Low: Requests requiring routine clinical attention.
Moderate: Requests requiring clinical assessment within an appropriate timeframe.
High: Requests requiring prompt clinical attention.
Critical: Requests requiring immediate clinical assessment or emergency escalation.

The project will investigate the relationships between patient characteristics, reported symptoms, clinical measurements, and clinician-assigned urgency categories through exploratory data analysis and statistical hypothesis testing.
The statistical analysis will help establish whether observed differences and associations across urgency categories are statistically significant.
Machine learning experiments will subsequently investigate whether the available patient intake information can support the classification of requests into the four urgency categories.
The project will also examine the consequences of incorrect predictions, particularly under-triage, where a request requiring a higher level of attention is assigned a lower urgency category.
A Streamlit dashboard will be developed to present the analytical findings, hypothesis testing results, model evaluation metrics, and relevant visualizations through an interactive interface.

The model will serve as an experimental decision-support approach. It will not independently diagnose patients, prescribe treatment, or replace clinical judgment. Emergency warning signs must remain subject to appropriate clinical escalation procedures.

To investigate patient intake patterns through exploratory data analysis and statistical hypothesis testing, develop and evaluate a machine learning classification model for estimating telemedicine request urgency, and build an interactive Streamlit dashboard for presenting analytical findings and model evaluation results.

The project covers the experimental development of a machine learning model for telemedicine request urgency classification.

The project will conclude with an experimentally evaluated machine learning model, an interactive Streamlit analytical dashboard, and supporting documentation.

The project will use a structured dataset representing the telemedicine triage process, from the initial submission of a patient's request to the clinician's assessment and the model's urgency prediction.
The dataset will consist of three interconnected tables: patient_intake, triage_assessments, and model_predictions.
The dataset will represent information collected through Nexora Care's telemedicine intake process and subsequent clinical assessments.
Patient intake records will contain demographic information, reported complaints, symptoms, medical history, selected warning signs, existing medical conditions, and available vital signs.
Clinical assessment records will contain the urgency level assigned by the reviewing clinician.
Model prediction records will capture the urgency classification, associated probabilities, and prioritization score generated from the patient's intake information.
This table contains the information submitted by the patient when creating a telemedicine request through the app.
Unique identifier for each telemedicine request
Main reason for seeking medical attention, selected from predefined categories
Relevant medical history provided by the patient
Multiple warning signs selected by the patient
Existing medical conditions selected by the patient
Additional description of symptoms and health concerns
Date and time the request was submitted
The red_flags and comorbidities fields will accommodate multiple selections through dropdown or multi-select inputs in the telemedicine application.
During data preprocessing, these fields will be transformed into individual binary features using multi-hot encoding.
For example, a patient selecting chest pain and breathing difficulty will have both conditions represented as separate binary features after encoding.

Vital signs will be stored as individual numerical fields. Blood pressure will be separated into systolic and diastolic measurements during preprocessing to make both values independently available for modelling.
Missing vital sign measurements will be permitted where patients do not have access to the required measuring devices and will be handled appropriately during data preparation.
Categorical fields such as chief_complaint_category, sex, and pregnancy_flag will undergo appropriate encoding.
The symptom_description field may also undergo text preprocessing and feature extraction as part of the modelling experiments.
This table contains the clinical assessment performed after a nurse or clinician reviews the patient's telemedicine request.
The clinician's assessment provides the reference urgency classification used as the target variable during supervised model training.
Unique identifier for each clinical assessment
Identifier linking the assessment to the patient request
Identifier of the nurse or clinician performing the assessment
Indicates whether further clinical escalation is required
Date and time the assessment was completed
Clinical protocol or guideline used during assessment
This table records the output generated by the trained machine learning model for each telemedicine request.
Unique identifier for each model prediction
Identifier linking the prediction to the patient request
Urgency category predicted by the model
Score generated to support queue prioritization
Version of the model that generated the prediction
Date and time the prediction was generated
The target variable for the supervised machine learning task will be clinical_urgency, obtained from the triage_assessments table.
It will represent the urgency level assigned by a clinician following the review of a patient's telemedicine request.
The target variable will contain four classification categories:
Low: Non-urgent complaints that can generally be handled through routine care.
Moderate: Complaints requiring timely attention but not necessarily immediate intervention.
High: Complaints requiring prompt clinical attention.
Critical: Complaints requiring immediate clinical attention and appropriate emergency escalation.
The model will learn the relationship between the information in patient_intake and the clinician-assigned urgency category in triage_assessments.

Its input features will include demographic information, complaint details, encoded red flags, encoded comorbidities, available vital signs, and potentially extracted features from the symptom description.
During prediction, it will use only the intake information available at the time of submission to estimate the patient's urgency and generate a prioritization score.

Information recorded after the initial patient submission, including clinician assessment notes and assessor details, must not be used as model input features when predicting urgency before clinical review.

The prioritization score will be derived using a documented scoring approach based on the model's prediction outputs. It will serve as an experimental decision-support measure and will not be treated as a clinically validated measure of patient risk.
Red-flag responses must also be handled through appropriate clinical escalation protocols independently of the model's prediction.

The project will follow eight experimental phases, progressing from data preparation and statistical analysis to machine learning experimentation, model evaluation, and dashboard development.

This phase will investigate whether observed differences and relationships between patient intake characteristics and clinical urgency are statistically significant.
The analysis will use appropriate statistical tests based on variable types, data distributions, sample sizes, and test assumptions.
The significance level will be set at 0.05.
The following hypotheses will guide the statistical analysis.
Hypothesis 1: Patient Age and Clinical Urgency
H0: There is no statistically significant difference in patient age across the four clinical urgency categories.
H1: There is a statistically significant difference in patient age across at least two clinical urgency categories.
Proposed test: Kruskal-Wallis H test, with one-way ANOVA considered where its assumptions are satisfied.
H0: There is no statistically significant association between patient sex and clinical urgency.
H1: There is a statistically significant association between patient sex and clinical urgency.
Proposed test: Chi-square test of independence.
Hypothesis 3: Chief Complaint Category and Clinical Urgency
H0: Chief complaint category is independent of clinical urgency.
H1: Chief complaint category is significantly associated with clinical urgency.
Proposed test: Chi-square test of independence.
Hypothesis 4: Symptom Severity and Clinical Urgency
H0: There is no statistically significant difference in reported symptom severity across clinical urgency categories.
H1: There is a statistically significant difference in reported symptom severity across at least two clinical urgency categories.
Proposed test: Kruskal-Wallis H test for ordinal severity measurements.
Hypothesis 5: Red Flags and Clinical Urgency
H0: The presence of reported red flags is not significantly associated with clinical urgency.
H1: The presence of reported red flags is significantly associated with clinical urgency.
Proposed test: Chi-square test of independence.
Individual red flags, including breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion, severe bleeding, seizure, and stroke signs, may also be investigated separately.
H0: There is no statistically significant association between reported comorbidities and clinical urgency.
H1: There is a statistically significant association between reported comorbidities and clinical urgency.
Proposed test: Chi-square test of independence.
Hypothesis 7: Oxygen Saturation and Clinical Urgency
H0: There is no statistically significant difference in oxygen saturation across the four clinical urgency categories.
H1: There is a statistically significant difference in oxygen saturation across at least two clinical urgency categories.
Hypothesis 8: Heart Rate and Clinical Urgency
H0: There is no statistically significant difference in heart rate across the four clinical urgency categories.
H1: There is a statistically significant difference in heart rate across at least two clinical urgency categories.
Hypothesis 9: Symptom Duration and Clinical Urgency
H0: There is no statistically significant difference in symptom duration across clinical urgency categories.
H1: There is a statistically significant difference in symptom duration across at least two clinical urgency categories.
Proposed test: Kruskal-Wallis H test, depending on how symptom duration is represented.

Tukey's HSD for appropriate ANOVA comparisons.
Pairwise proportion comparisons where categorical analysis requires them.

Model selection will be based on the overall evaluation framework rather than accuracy alone. Particular importance will be given to the model's ability to recognize requests assigned to High and Critical urgency categories.

The final outcome of the Nexora Care Triage Prioritization project will be an experimentally developed and evaluated machine learning classification model capable of estimating the urgency category of incoming telemedicine requests using patient intake and symptom-related information.

The project will demonstrate how statistical analysis and machine learning can be applied to investigate patient-reported symptoms, demographic characteristics, medical history, and available vital signs to understand and estimate request urgency across Low, Moderate, High, and Critical categories.
Exploratory data analysis and statistical hypothesis testing will provide insights into the relationships between patient intake characteristics and clinician-assigned urgency levels.
Different classification algorithms will be evaluated and compared, with attention given to category-specific performance, under-triage errors, and the reliability of model predictions.

An interactive Streamlit dashboard will provide a centralized interface for exploring the dataset, examining statistical findings, reviewing model performance, investigating classification errors, understanding feature contributions, and demonstrating experimental model predictions.
The resulting model, analytical findings, and dashboard will provide Nexora Care with an experimental foundation for exploring data-driven telemedicine request prioritization.

The model will remain an experimental decision-support model and will not independently determine clinical urgency or replace qualified healthcare professionals. Any future use within Nexora Care Flow will require appropriate clinical validation, governance, emergency escalation procedures, and human oversight.
